newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. payrolls hog pre-election stage.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. payrolls hog pre-election stage.

text.p: The world's most closely watched economic indicator will hog the limelight next Friday when October non-farm payroll figures cap a prolific week for U.S. data only four days before the presidential election.
Markets are gearing up for a significant rebound after September's surprise fall of 40,000.

"Bond markets will be nervous going into next week's figures, which will hold back gains in the dollar and provide a nervous backdrop for price action in the stock market, especially on Wall Street," said Neil Mackinnon at Citibank.

Mackinnon, chief economist at the U.S. bank, said October payrolls growth was likely to exceed 200,000 and the September figure might be revised up. He described the September data as an aberration due to special factors on teacher employment.

"The big picture is that the U.S. economy is in good shape. We saw this on Friday with durable goods orders (up 4.6 percent for September)," said Mackinnon, adding that latest indicators were consistent with a tighter labour market.
Ken Wattret, economist at Paribas Capital Markets, said the payrolls number was part of a deluge of U.S. data whose other highlights include third quarter GDP figures due on Wednesday.
They also include, and personal income and spending data for September on Thursday.

GDP grew 4.7 percent in the second quarter and Wattret said he was looking for the new figure to come in at 2.25 percent. "This would be encouraging for US Treasuries, but a strong payrolls figure and some strong labour market data could undermine any positive sentiment within a couple of days."

In Europe, analysts said guessing games over the Bundesbank's intentions on interest rates might continue because it suited the German central bank to keep markets on their toes by feeding them ambiguous comments.

"In the near term I would guess there will be no change in rates, but the Buba is quite happy to keep alive market hopes of a cut which is all part of its preference for a strong dollar," Mackinnon said.
Elsewhere in Europe, analysts saw scope for some interest rate cuts following those seen this week in Italy and Sweden.
"Further cuts could come through in Italy. There is still scope for high yielders to reduce," Mackinnon said.
Wattret said further cuts in Italy were still one or two months away because the central bank did not want to give the impression of slashing rates too quickly.
However, he said one possibility was that France might trim five to 10 basis points off its five to 10 day rate if the French franc stayed strong.

Any cut, Wattrett said, would certainly be portrayed as being in response to the strength of the currency rather than an expected further deterioration in France's 12.6 percent unemployment rate when September data are released on Thursday.

Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic advisor at BankAmerica, noted a US quarterly refunding release Wednesday. "People will be looking for an increase in participation coming out of Japan which should lead to additional downside pressure on the yen."

In Britain, Hawkins said the purchasing managers survey and consumer credit data were expected to fit in with the view that the economy was accelerating, leading to speculation that interest rates might have to rise before the 1997 election.
But Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke would turn down any rate hike request from Bank of England governor Eddie George when the two have their monthly meeting on Wednesday, Hawkins added.
